claim: Firefly luciferase is widely used in biotechnology.
source: Today firefly luciferase is widely used in biotechnology, but the evolutionary origin of bioluminescence within beetles remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as established fact in the abstract without specific data in this manuscript, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: The evolutionary origin of bioluminescence within beetles remains unclear.
source: Today firefly luciferase is widely used in biotechnology, but the evolutionary origin of bioluminescence within beetles remains unclear.
evidence: This statement frames the research question and is supported by the subsequent discussion of competing hypotheses.

claim: Photinus pyralis and Aquatica lateralis diverged over 100 million years ago.
source: To shed light on this long-standing question, we sequenced the genomes of two firefly species that diverged over 100 million-years-ago: the North American Photinus pyralis and Japanese Aquatica lateralis.
evidence: This temporal claim is supported by phylogenetic dating referenced in the manuscript (Misof et al., 2014; Mckenna et al., 2015).

claim: Ignelater luminosus has bioluminescent biochemistry near-identical to fireflies.
source: To compare bioluminescent origins, we also sequenced the genome of a related click beetle, the Caribbean Ignelater luminosus, with bioluminescent biochemistry near-identical to fireflies, but anatomically unique light organs, suggesting the intriguing hypothesis of parallel gains of bioluminescence.
evidence: This is stated as known fact and is consistent with established biochemical knowledge about beetle bioluminescence.

claim: Ignelater luminosus has anatomically unique light organs compared to fireflies.
source: To compare bioluminescent origins, we also sequenced the genome of a related click beetle, the Caribbean Ignelater luminosus, with bioluminescent biochemistry near-identical to fireflies, but anatomically unique light organs, suggesting the intriguing hypothesis of parallel gains of bioluminescence.
evidence: This anatomical difference is described and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The analyses support independent gains of bioluminescence in fireflies and click beetles.
source: Our analyses support independent gains of bioluminescence in fireflies and click beetles, and provide new insights into the genes, chemical defenses, and symbionts that evolved alongside their luminous lifestyle.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by genomic synteny analysis, ancestral state reconstruction, and molecular evolution analyses presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Firefly luminous courtship displays have been studied for their role in mate recognition.
source: The coded language of their luminous courtship displays (Figure 1A; Video 1) has been long studied for its role in mate recognition (Lloyd, 1966; Lewis and Cratsley, 2008; Stanger-Hall and Lloyd, 2015), while non-adult bioluminescence is likely a warning signal of their unpalatable chemical defenses (De Cock and Matthysen, 1999), such as the cardiotoxic lucibufagins of Photinus fireflies (Meinwald et al., 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Non-adult firefly bioluminescence is likely a warning signal of unpalatable chemical defenses.
source: The coded language of their luminous courtship displays (Figure 1A; Video 1) has been long studied for its role in mate recognition (Lloyd, 1966; Lewis and Cratsley, 2008; Stanger-Hall and Lloyd, 2015), while non-adult bioluminescence is likely a warning signal of their unpalatable chemical defenses (De Cock and Matthysen, 1999), such as the cardiotoxic lucibufagins of Photinus fireflies (Meinwald et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Cock and Matthysen, 1999.

claim: Photinus fireflies contain cardiotoxic lucibufagins.
source: The coded language of their luminous courtship displays (Figure 1A; Video 1) has been long studied for its role in mate recognition (Lloyd, 1966; Lewis and Cratsley, 2008; Stanger-Hall and Lloyd, 2015), while non-adult bioluminescence is likely a warning signal of their unpalatable chemical defenses (De Cock and Matthysen, 1999), such as the cardiotoxic lucibufagins of Photinus fireflies (Meinwald et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meinwald et al., 1979, and confirmed by LC-HRAM-MS data in this study (Figure 6B).

claim: Firefly luminescence is an ATP, Mg2+, and O2-dependent luciferase-mediated oxidation of luciferin.
source: The biochemical understanding of firefly luminescence: an ATP, Mg2+, and O2-dependent luciferase-mediated oxidation of the substrate luciferin (Shimomura, 2012), along with the cloning of the luciferase gene (de Wet et al., 1985; Ow et al., 1986), led to the widespread use of luciferase as a reporter with unique applications in biomedical research and industry (Fraga, 2008).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge cited from Shimomura, 2012.

claim: The firefly luciferase gene was cloned.
source: The biochemical understanding of firefly luminescence: an ATP, Mg2+, and O2-dependent luciferase-mediated oxidation of the substrate luciferin (Shimomura, 2012), along with the cloning of the luciferase gene (de Wet et al., 1985; Ow et al., 1986), led to the widespread use of luciferase as a reporter with unique applications in biomedical research and industry (Fraga, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Wet et al., 1985 and Ow et al., 1986.

claim: Luciferase has unique applications in biomedical research and industry.
source: The biochemical understanding of firefly luminescence: an ATP, Mg2+, and O2-dependent luciferase-mediated oxidation of the substrate luciferin (Shimomura, 2012), along with the cloning of the luciferase gene (de Wet et al., 1985; Ow et al., 1986), led to the widespread use of luciferase as a reporter with unique applications in biomedical research and industry (Fraga, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fraga, 2008.

claim: There are over 2000 firefly species globally.
source: With >2000 species globally, fireflies are undoubtedly the most culturally appreciated bioluminescent group, yet there are at least three other beetle families with bioluminescent species: click beetles (Elateridae), American railroad worms (Phengodidae) and Asian starworms (Rhagophthalmidae) (Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about firefly diversity.

claim: There are at least three other beetle families with bioluminescent species besides fireflies: click beetles (Elateridae), American railroad worms (Phengodidae) and Asian starworms (Rhagophthalmidae).
source: With >2000 species globally, fireflies are undoubtedly the most culturally appreciated bioluminescent group, yet there are at least three other beetle families with bioluminescent species: click beetles (Elateridae), American railroad worms (Phengodidae) and Asian starworms (Rhagophthalmidae) (Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2017.

claim: The four bioluminescent beetle families have homologous luciferases and structurally identical luciferins.
source: These four closely related families (superfamily Elateroidea) have homologous luciferases and structurally identical luciferins (Shimomura, 2012), implying a single origin of beetle bioluminescence.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shimomura, 2012.

claim: The light organs amongst the luminous beetle families are clearly distinct.
source: However, as Darwin recognized in his 'Difficulties on Theory' (Darwin, 1872), the light organs amongst the luminous beetle families are clearly distinct (Figure 1B), implying independent origins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Darwin, 1872, and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: P. pyralis has well-developed ventral light organs on true abdominal segments 6 and 7.
source: Note the well-developed ventral light organs on the true abdominal segments 6 and 7 of P. pyralis and A. lateralis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with anatomical images.

claim: A. lateralis has well-developed ventral light organs on true abdominal segments 6 and 7.
source: Note the well-developed ventral light organs on the true abdominal segments 6 and 7 of P. pyralis and A. lateralis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with anatomical images.

claim: I. luminosus has paired dorsal light organs at the base of its prothorax.
source: In contrast, the luminescent click beetle, I. luminosus, has paired dorsal light organs at the base of its prothorax (arrowhead) and a lantern on the anterior surface of the ventral abdomen (not visible).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with anatomical images.

claim: I. luminosus has a lantern on the anterior surface of the ventral abdomen.
source: In contrast, the luminescent click beetle, I. luminosus, has paired dorsal light organs at the base of its prothorax (arrowhead) and a lantern on the anterior surface of the ventral abdomen (not visible).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing anatomical features.

claim: P. pyralis was used in classic studies of firefly bioluminescent biochemistry.
source: P. pyralis was used in classic studies of firefly bioluminescent biochemistry (Bitler and McElroy, 1957) and the cloning of luciferase (de Wet et al., 1985), while A. lateralis, a species with specialized aquatic larvae, is one of the few fireflies that can be reliably cultured in the laboratory (Oba et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bitler and McElroy, 1957.

claim: P. pyralis was used in the cloning of luciferase.
source: P. pyralis was used in classic studies of firefly bioluminescent biochemistry (Bitler and McElroy, 1957) and the cloning of luciferase (de Wet et al., 1985), while A. lateralis, a species with specialized aquatic larvae, is one of the few fireflies that can be reliably cultured in the laboratory (Oba et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to de Wet et al., 1985.

claim: A. lateralis has specialized aquatic larvae.
source: P. pyralis was used in classic studies of firefly bioluminescent biochemistry (Bitler and McElroy, 1957) and the cloning of luciferase (de Wet et al., 1985), while A. lateralis, a species with specialized aquatic larvae, is one of the few fireflies that can be reliably cultured in the laboratory (Oba et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of A. lateralis.

claim: A. lateralis is one of the few fireflies that can be reliably cultured in the laboratory.
source: P. pyralis was used in classic studies of firefly bioluminescent biochemistry (Bitler and McElroy, 1957) and the cloning of luciferase (de Wet et al., 1985), while A. lateralis, a species with specialized aquatic larvae, is one of the few fireflies that can be reliably cultured in the laboratory (Oba et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oba et al., 2013a.

claim: P. pyralis and A. lateralis represent the two major firefly subfamilies, Lampyrinae and Luciolinae.
source: These two fireflies represent the two major firefly subfamilies, Lampyrinae and Luciolinae, which diverged from a common ancestor over 100 Mya (Figure 1B) (Misof et al., 2014; Mckenna et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as taxonomic fact.

claim: Lampyrinae and Luciolinae diverged from a common ancestor over 100 Mya.
source: These two fireflies represent the two major firefly subfamilies, Lampyrinae and Luciolinae, which diverged from a common ancestor over 100 Mya (Figure 1B) (Misof et al., 2014; Mckenna et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Misof et al., 2014 and Mckenna et al., 2015.

claim: Raphaël Dubois used 'Pyrophorus' to establish the enzymatic basis of bioluminescence in the late 1800s.
source: To facilitate evolutionary comparisons, we also sequenced the 'Cucubano', Ignelater luminosus (Figure 1B), a Caribbean bioluminescent click beetle, and member of the 'Pyrophorus' used by Raphaël Dubois (1849-1929) to first establish the enzymatic basis of bioluminescence in the late 1800s (Dubois, 1885; Dubois, 1886).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dubois, 1885 and Dubois, 1886.

claim: P. pyralis adult males were collected from the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, USA and Mercer Meadows New Jersey, USA.
source: Photinus pyralis adult males were collected from the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, USA (GSMNP) and Mercer Meadows New Jersey, USA (MMNJ) (Figure 1C), and sequenced using short-insert, mate-pair, Hi-C, and long-read Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) approaches (Appendix 4—table 1).
evidence: This describes the sample collection for the study.

claim: P. pyralis was sequenced using short-insert, mate-pair, Hi-C, and long-read Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) approaches.
source: Photinus pyralis adult males were collected from the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, USA (GSMNP) and Mercer Meadows New Jersey, USA (MMNJ) (Figure 1C), and sequenced using short-insert, mate-pair, Hi-C, and long-read Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) approaches (Appendix 4—table 1).
evidence: This describes the sequencing methods used.

claim: The P. pyralis datasets were combined in a MaSuRCA hybrid genome assembly.
source: These datasets were combined in a MaSuRCA (Zimin et al., 2013) hybrid genome assembly (Appendix 1.5).
evidence: This describes the assembly method used.

claim: The A. lateralis genome was derived from an ALL-PATHs assembly of short insert and mate-pair reads from a single adult female.
source: The Aquatica lateralis genome was derived from an ALL-PATHs (Butler et al., 2008) assembly of short insert and mate-pair reads from a single adult female from a laboratory-reared population, whose lineage, dubbed 'Ikeya-Y90', was first collected 25 years ago from a now extinct population in Yokohama, Japan (Appendix 2.5).
evidence: This describes the assembly method and sample source.

claim: The A. lateralis 'Ikeya-Y90' lineage was first collected 25 years ago from a now extinct population in Yokohama, Japan.
source: The Aquatica lateralis genome was derived from an ALL-PATHs (Butler et al., 2008) assembly of short insert and mate-pair reads from a single adult female from a laboratory-reared population, whose lineage, dubbed 'Ikeya-Y90', was first collected 25 years ago from a now extinct population in Yokohama, Japan (Appendix 2.5).
evidence: This provides historical information about the sample lineage.

claim: A single I. luminosus adult male collected in Mayagüez Puerto Rico, USA, was used to produce a high-coverage Supernova linked-read draft genome.
source: A single Ignelater luminosus adult male, collected in Mayagüez Puerto Rico, USA, was used to produce a high-coverage Supernova (Weisenfeld et al., 2017) linked-read draft genome (Appendix 3.5), which was further manually scaffolded using low-coverage long-read Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencing (Appendix 3.5.4).
evidence: This describes the sample and assembly method.

claim: The I. luminosus genome was further manually scaffolded using low-coverage long-read Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencing.
source: A single Ignelater luminosus adult male, collected in Mayagüez Puerto Rico, USA, was used to produce a high-coverage Supernova (Weisenfeld et al., 2017) linked-read draft genome (Appendix 3.5), which was further manually scaffolded using low-coverage long-read Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencing (Appendix 3.5.4).
evidence: This describes additional assembly refinement.

claim: The gene completeness and contiguity statistics of P. pyralis (Ppyr1.3) and A. lateralis (Alat1.3) genome assemblies are comparable to the genome of the model beetle Tribolium castaneum.
source: The gene completeness and contiguity statistics of our P. pyralis (Ppyr1.3) and A. lateralis (Alat1.3) genome assemblies are comparable to the genome of the model beetle Tribolium castaneum (Figure 2F; Appendix 4.1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The I. luminosus genome assembly (Ilumi1.2) is less complete than P. pyralis and A. lateralis, but is comparable to other published insect genomes.
source: The I. luminosus genome assembly (Ilumi1.2) is less complete, but is comparable to other published insect genomes (Figure 2F; Appendix 4.1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus coding gene annotation sets contain 94.2%, 90.0%, and 91.8% of the Endopterygota BUSCOs, respectively.
source: These coding gene annotation sets for P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus are comprised of 15,773, 14,285, and 27,557 genes containing 94.2%, 90.0%, and 91.8% of the Endopterygota Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCOs) (Simão et al., 2015), respectively.
evidence: This provides quantitative assessment of annotation completeness using BUSCO analysis.

claim: 77% of genes were found in orthogroups with at least one other species.
source: Protein clustering via predicted orthology indicated 77% of genes were found in orthogroups with at least one other species (Figure 2E; Appendix 4—figure 1).
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The greatest orthogroup overlap was found between the P. pyralis and A. lateralis genesets.
source: We found the greatest orthogroup overlap between the P. pyralis and A. lateralis genesets, as expected given the more recent phylogenetic divergence of these species.
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis and is consistent with phylogenetic expectations.

claim: Remaining redundancy in the P. pyralis assembly is likely due to the heterozygosity of the outbred input libraries.
source: Remaining redundancy in the P. pyralis assembly and annotation, as indicated by duplicates of the BUSCOs and the assembly size (Figure 2F; Appendix 4—table 2) is likely due to the heterozygosity of the outbred input libraries (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on assembly characteristics and knowledge of the sample source.

claim: The P. pyralis genome assembly was super-scaffolded into 11 pseudo-chromosomal linkage groups using Hi-C proximity-ligation linkage approach.
source: To enable the characterization of long-range genetic structure, we super-scaffolded the P. pyralis genome assembly into 11 pseudo-chromosomal linkage groups using a Hi-C proximity-ligation linkage approach (Figure 2A; Appendix 1.5.3).
evidence: This describes the scaffolding method and is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 11 P. pyralis linkage groups contain 95% of the assembly (448.8 Mbp).
source: These linkage groups contain 95% of the assembly (448.8 Mbp).
evidence: This provides quantitative information about the scaffolding results.

claim: Linkage group LG3a corresponds to the X-chromosome based on expected adult XO male read coverage and gene content.
source: Linkage group LG3a corresponds to the X-chromosome based on expected adult XO male read coverage and gene content (Appendix 1.6.4.1) and its size (22.2 Mbp) is comparable to the expected X-chromosome size based on sex-specific genome size estimates using flow cytometry (~26 Mbp) (Lower et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on coverage analysis and gene content analysis.

claim: The P. pyralis X-chromosome size (22.2 Mbp) is comparable to the expected X-chromosome size based on sex-specific genome size estimates using flow cytometry (~26 Mbp).
source: Linkage group LG3a corresponds to the X-chromosome based on expected adult XO male read coverage and gene content (Appendix 1.6.4.1) and its size (22.2 Mbp) is comparable to the expected X-chromosome size based on sex-specific genome size estimates using flow cytometry (~26 Mbp) (Lower et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lower et al., 2017 and comparison of assembly data to flow cytometry estimates.

claim: Homologs to T. castaneum X-chromosome genes were enriched on LG3a over every other linkage group.
source: Homologs to T. castaneum X-chromosome genes were enriched on LG3a over every other linkage group, suggesting that the X-chromosomes of these distantly related beetles are homologous, and that their content has been reasonably conserved for >200 MY (Appendix 1.6.4.1) (Mckenna et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The X-chromosomes of P. pyralis and T. castaneum are homologous, and their content has been reasonably conserved for >200 MY.
source: Homologs to T. castaneum X-chromosome genes were enriched on LG3a over every other linkage group, suggesting that the X-chromosomes of these distantly related beetles are homologous, and that their content has been reasonably conserved for >200 MY (Appendix 1.6.4.1) (Mckenna et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene content analysis and supported by phylogenetic dating from Mckenna et al., 2015.

claim: P. pyralis Luc1 and LST are located on separate linkage groups.
source: We hypothesized that the P. pyralis orthologs of known bioluminescence genes, including the canonical luciferase Luc1 (de Wet et al., 1985) and the specialized luciferin sulfotransferase LST (Fallon et al., 2016), would be located on the same linkage group to facilitate chromosomal looping and enhancer assisted co-expression within the light organ. We, however, found these genes on separate linkage groups (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and contradicts the initial hypothesis.

claim: The complete mitochondrial genomes of P. pyralis and I. luminosus were assembled.
source: In addition to nuclear genome assembly and coding gene annotation, we also assembled the complete mitochondrial genomes (mtDNA) of P. pyralis (Figure 2C; Appendix 1.8) and I. luminosus (Appendix 3.10), while the mtDNA sequence of A. lateralis was recently published (Maeda et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the mitochondrial genome assembly work.

claim: The mtDNA sequence of A. lateralis was recently published.
source: In addition to nuclear genome assembly and coding gene annotation, we also assembled the complete mitochondrial genomes (mtDNA) of P. pyralis (Figure 2C; Appendix 1.8) and I. luminosus (Appendix 3.10), while the mtDNA sequence of A. lateralis was recently published (Maeda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maeda et al., 2017.

claim: The mtDNA assemblies show high conservation of gene content and synteny, with the exception of the variable ~1 Kbp tandem repeat unit (TRU) found in the firefly mtDNAs.
source: These mtDNA assemblies show high conservation of gene content and synteny, with the exception of the variable ~1 Kbp tandem repeat unit (TRU) found in the firefly mtDNAs.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of the assembled mitochondrial genomes.

claim: 42.6%, 19.8%, and 34.1% of the P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus assemblies were found to be repetitive, respectively.
source: Overall, 42.6%, 19.8%, and 34.1% of the P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus assemblies were found to be repetitive, respectively (Appendix 1.11; 2.9; 3.9).
evidence: This provides quantitative data on repeat content.

claim: 66.7%, 39.4%, and 55% of repeats in P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus could not be classified as any known repetitive sequence, respectively.
source: Of these repeats 66.7%, 39.4%, and 55% could not be classified as any known repetitive sequence, respectively.
evidence: This provides quantitative data on unclassified repeat content.

claim: Helitrons are among the most abundant individual repeat elements in the P. pyralis assembly.
source: Helitrons, DNA transposons that transpose through rolling circle replication (Kapitonov and Jurka, 2001), are among the most abundant individual repeat elements in the P. pyralis assembly.
evidence: This is based on repeat annotation analysis.

claim: P. pyralis chromosomes have canonical telomeres with telomeric repeats (TTAGG).
source: Via in situ hybridization, we identified that P. pyralis chromosomes have canonical telomeres with telomeric repeats (TTAGG) (Figure 2B; Appendix 1.13).
evidence: This is shown by FISH data in Figure 2B.

claim: Methylation at CpGs (mCG) was unambiguously detected at ~20% within the genic regions of P. pyralis.
source: Methylation at CpGs (mCG) was unambiguously detected at ~20% within the genic regions of P. pyralis and its methylation levels were at least twice those reported from other holometabolous insects (Figure 2D; Appendix 1.12).
evidence: This is based on whole genome bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: P. pyralis methylation levels were at least twice those reported from other holometabolous insects.
source: Methylation at CpGs (mCG) was unambiguously detected at ~20% within the genic regions of P. pyralis and its methylation levels were at least twice those reported from other holometabolous insects (Figure 2D; Appendix 1.12).
evidence: This is based on comparison of WGBS data to published data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Direct orthologs of both DNMT1 and DNMT3 were conserved in P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus.
source: Molecular evolution analyses of the DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) show that direct orthologs of both DNMT1 and DNMT3 were conserved in P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus (Appendix 4—figure 2; Appendix 4.2.3), implying that our three study species, and inferentially likely most firefly lineages, possess mCG.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of DNMT genes.

claim: The three study species, and inferentially likely most firefly lineages, possess mCG.
source: Molecular evolution analyses of the DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) show that direct orthologs of both DNMT1 and DNMT3 were conserved in P. pyralis, A. lateralis, and I. luminosus (Appendix 4—figure 2; Appendix 4.2.3), implying that our three study species, and inferentially likely most firefly lineages, possess mCG.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of DNMT genes and CpG[O/E] analysis.

claim: Two luciferase paralogs have been previously described in fireflies.
source: Two luciferase paralogs have been previously described in fireflies (Oba et al., 2013a; Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oba et al., 2013a and Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017.

claim: P. pyralis Luc1 was the first firefly luciferase cloned.
source: P. pyralis Luc1 was the first firefly luciferase cloned (de Wet et al., 1985), and its direct orthologs have been widely identified from other fireflies (Oba, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to de Wet et al., 1985.

claim: Direct orthologs of P. pyralis Luc1 have been widely identified from other fireflies.
source: P. pyralis Luc1 was the first firefly luciferase cloned (de Wet et al., 1985), and its direct orthologs have been widely identified from other fireflies (Oba, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oba, 2014.

claim: Luc2 was previously known only from a handful of Asian taxa, including A. lateralis.
source: The luciferase paralog Luc2 was previously known only from a handful of Asian taxa, including A. lateralis (Oba et al., 2013a; Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oba et al., 2013a and Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017.

claim: In Asian taxa, Luc1 is responsible for light production from the lanterns of adults, larvae, prepupae and pupae.
source: Previous investigations of these Asian taxa have shown that Luc1 is responsible for light production from the lanterns of adults, larvae, prepupae and pupae, whereas Luc2 is responsible for the dim glow of eggs, ovaries, prepupae and the whole pupal body (Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017.

claim: In Asian taxa, Luc2 is responsible for the dim glow of eggs, ovaries, prepupae and the whole pupal body.
source: Previous investigations of these Asian taxa have shown that Luc1 is responsible for light production from the lanterns of adults, larvae, prepupae and pupae, whereas Luc2 is responsible for the dim glow of eggs, ovaries, prepupae and the whole pupal body (Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017.

claim: Two firefly luciferases, Luc1 and Luc2, were unequivocally identified in both the P. pyralis and A. lateralis genomes.
source: From our curated genesets (Appendix 1.10; 2.8), we unequivocally identified two firefly luciferases, Luc1 and Luc2, in both the P. pyralis and A. lateralis genomes.
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and curation.

claim: In both P. pyralis and A. lateralis, Luc1 is the sole luciferase expressed in the lanterns of both larvae and adults, regardless of sex.
source: Our RNA-Seq data further show that in both P. pyralis and A. lateralis, Luc1 and Luc2 display expression patterns consistent with previous reports. While Luc1 is the sole luciferase expressed in the lanterns of both larvae and adults, regardless of sex, Luc2 is expressed in other tissues and stages, such as eggs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In both P. pyralis and A. lateralis, Luc2 is expressed in other tissues and stages, such as eggs.
source: Our RNA-Seq data further show that in both P. pyralis and A. lateralis, Luc1 and Luc2 display expression patterns consistent with previous reports. While Luc1 is the sole luciferase expressed in the lanterns of both larvae and adults, regardless of sex, Luc2 is expressed in other tissues and stages, such as eggs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Luc2 expression is detected in RNA libraries derived from adult female bodies (without head or lantern), suggesting detection of ovary expression.
source: Notably, Luc2 expression is detected in RNA libraries derived from adult female bodies (without head or lantern), suggesting detection of ovary expression as described in previous studies (Bessho-Uehara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data and is consistent with previous reports cited.

claim: Since their divergence via gene duplication prior to the divergence of Lampyrinae and Luciolinae, Luc1 and Luc2 have established different, but conserved roles in bioluminescence throughout the firefly life cycle.
source: Together, these results support that since their divergence via gene duplication prior to the divergence of Lampyrinae and Luciolinae, Luc1 and Luc2 have established different, but conserved roles in bioluminescence throughout the firefly life cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on expression data and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Firefly luciferase is hypothesized to be derived from an ancestral peroxisomal fatty acyl-CoA synthetase (PACS).
source: Firefly luciferase is hypothesized to be derived from an ancestral peroxisomal fatty acyl-CoA synthetase (PACS) (Figure 3A) (Oba et al., 2003; Oba et al., 2006a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oba et al., 2003 and Oba et al., 2006a.

claim: In both firefly species, Luc1 is genomically clustered with its closely related homologs, including PACSs and non-peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSs).
source: We found that, in both firefly species, Luc1 is genomically clustered with its closely related homologs, including PACSs and non-peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSs), enzymes which can be distinguished by the presence/absence of a C-terminal peroxisomal-targeting-signal-1 (PTS1).
evidence: This is based on genomic synteny analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Microsomal glutathione S-transferase (MGST) family genes were found nearby Luc1 and are directly orthologous between both firefly species.
source: We also found nearby microsomal glutathione S-transferase (MGST) family genes (Figure 3D) that are directly orthologous between both species,
evidence: This is based on genomic synteny analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Luc1 and Luc2 are highly conserved at the level of gene structure—both are composed of seven exons with completely conserved exon/intron boundaries.
source: Luc1 and Luc2 are highly conserved at the level of gene structure—both are composed of seven exons with completely conserved exon/intron boundaries (Appendix 4—figure 4; Appendix 4—figure 5), and most members of Clades A, B, and C also have seven exons.
evidence: This is based on gene structure analysis.

claim: Most members of Clades A, B, and C also have seven exons.
source: Luc1 and Luc2 are highly conserved at the level of gene structure—both are composed of seven exons with completely conserved exon/intron boundaries (Appendix 4—figure 4; Appendix 4—figure 5), and most members of Clades A, B, and C also have seven exons.
evidence: This is based on gene structure analysis.

claim: Luc2 is located on a different linkage-group from Luc1 in P. pyralis and on a different scaffold from Luc1 in A. lateralis.
source: Luc2 is located on a different linkage-group from Luc1 in P. pyralis and on a different scaffold from Luc1 in A. lateralis, consistent with the interpretation that Luc1 and Luc2 lie on different chromosomes in both firefly species.
evidence: This is based on genomic location data.

claim: No PACS or ACS genes were found in the vicinity of Luc2 in either firefly species.
source: No PACS or ACS genes were found in the vicinity of Luc2 in either species.
evidence: This is based on genomic synteny analysis.

claim: Tandem gene duplication in a firefly ancestor gave rise to several ancestral PACS paralogs, one of which neofunctionalized in place to become the ancestral luciferase (AncLuc).
source: These data support that tandem gene duplication in a firefly ancestor gave rise to several ancestral PACS paralogs, one of which neofunctionalized in place to become the ancestral luciferase (AncLuc) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an evolutionary model inferred from synteny and phylogenetic data, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Prior to the divergence of the firefly subfamilies Lampyrinae and Luciolinae around 100 Mya, AncLuc duplicated, possibly via a long-range gene duplication event, and then subfunctionalized to give rise to Luc2, while the original AncLuc subfunctionalized in place to give rise to Luc1.
source: Prior to the divergence of the firefly subfamilies Lampyrinae and Luciolinae around 100 Mya (Appendix 4.3), this AncLuc duplicated, possibly via a long-range gene duplication event (e.g. transposon mobilization), and then subfunctionalized in its transcript expression pattern to give rise to Luc2, while the original AncLuc subfunctionalized in place to give rise to Luc1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an evolutionary model inferred from synteny, phylogenetic, and expression data, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: A single luciferase was identified in the I. luminosus genome which was highly expressed in both the dorsal prothorax and ventral abdominal lanterns.
source: Unlike some other described bioluminescent Elateridae, which have separate luciferases expressed in the dorsal prothorax and ventral abdominal lanterns (Oba et al., 2010a), we identified only a single luciferase in the I. luminosus genome which was highly expressed in both of the lanterns (Figure 3C; Appendix 3.8).
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and RNA-Seq expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The exon number and exon-intron splice junctions of IlumLuc are identical to those of firefly luciferases.
source: The exon number and exon-intron splice junctions of IlumLuc are identical to those of firefly luciferases, but unlike the firefly luciferases which have short introns less than <100 bp long, IlumLuc has two long introns (Appendix 4—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on gene structure analysis.

claim: IlumLuc has two long introns, unlike firefly luciferases which have short introns less than 100 bp long.
source: The exon number and exon-intron splice junctions of IlumLuc are identical to those of firefly luciferases, but unlike the firefly luciferases which have short introns less than <100 bp long, IlumLuc has two long introns (Appendix 4—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on gene structure analysis.

claim: Several PACS genes in the I. luminosus genome were related to IlumLuc and formed a clade (Clade D) specific to the Elateridae.
source: We found several PACS genes in the I. luminosus genome which were related to IlumLuc and formed a clade (Clade D) specific to the Elateridae (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The IlumLuc locus is not orthologous to the extant firefly Luc1 locus.
source: We infer that the IlumLuc locus is not orthologous to the extant firefly Luc1 locus, as IlumLuc is not physically clustered with Clade A, B or C ACS or PACS genes (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is an inference based on synteny analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A different scaffold in I. luminosus (Scaffold 9654) is likely orthologous to the firefly Luc1 locus.
source: We instead identified a different scaffold in I. luminosus that is likely orthologous to the firefly Luc1 locus (Scaffold 9654; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference based on synteny analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The genomic structures are consistent with independent origins of firefly and click beetle luciferases.
source: Overall, these genomic structures are consistent with independent origins of firefly and click beetle luciferases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on synteny analysis.

claim: Ancestral state reconstruction recovers at least two gains of luciferase activity in bioluminescent beetles.
source: We then carried out targeted molecular evolution analyses including the known beetle luciferases and their closely related homologs. Ancestral state reconstruction of luminescent activity on the gene tree using Mesquite (Maddison and Maddison, 2017) recovered two independent gains of luminescence as the most parsimonious and likely scenario: once in click beetles, and once in the common ancestor of firefly, phengodid, and rhagophthalmid beetles (Figure 4A; Appendix 4.3.3).
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 35% of the sites of the branch leading to the ancestral click beetle luciferase showed a statistically significant signal of episodic positive selection with dN/dS > 1 (ω or max dN/dS = 3.98).
source: In an independent molecular adaptation analysis utilizing the coding nucleotide sequence of the elaterid luciferases and their close homologs within Elateridae, 35% of the sites of the branch leading to the ancestral click beetle luciferase showed a statistically significant signal of episodic positive selection with dN/dS > 1 (ω or max dN/dS = 3.98) as compared to the evolution of its paralogs using the aBSREL branch-site selection test (Smith et al., 2015) (Figure 4B; Appendix 4.3.4).
evidence: This is based on molecular adaptation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The common ancestor of the click beetle luciferases (EAncLuc) underwent a period of accelerated directional evolution.
source: This implies that the common ancestor of the click beetle luciferases (EAncLuc) underwent a period of accelerated directional evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive selection signal detected.

claim: The identified selection signal represents the relatively recent neofunctionalization of click beetle luciferase from a non-luminous ancestral Clade D PACS gene.
source: As the branch under selection in the molecular adaptation analysis (Figure 4B) is the same branch of luciferase activity gain via ancestral reconstruction (Figure 4A), we conclude that the identified selection signal represents the relatively recent neofunctionalization of click beetle luciferase from a non-luminous ancestral Clade D PACS gene, distinct from the more ancient neofunctionalization of firefly luciferase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on integration of ancestral state reconstruction and molecular adaptation analyses.

claim: The neofunctionalization of EAncLuc occurred after the divergence of the elaterid subfamily Agrypninae.
source: Based on the constraints from our tree, we determine that this neofunctionalization of EAncLuc occured after the divergence of the elaterid subfamily Agrypninae.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic constraints.

claim: There is evidence for a subsequent luciferase duplication event in phengodids, but not in rhagophthalmids, that is independent of the duplication event that gave rise to Luc1 and Luc2 in fireflies.
source: There is evidence for a subsequent luciferase duplication event in phengodids, but not in rhagophthalmids, that is independent of the duplication event that gave rise to Luc1 and Luc2 in fireflies (Figures 3C and 4).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figures 3C and 4.

claim: The results strongly support the independent neofunctionalization of luciferase activity in click beetles and fireflies.
source: Altogether, our results strongly support the independent neofunctionalization of luciferase activity in click beetles and fireflies, and therefore at least two independent gains of luciferin-utilizing luminescence in beetles.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: There were at least two independent gains of luciferin-utilizing luminescence in beetles.
source: Altogether, our results strongly support the independent neofunctionalization of luciferase activity in click beetles and fireflies, and therefore at least two independent gains of luciferin-utilizing luminescence in beetles.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The enzymes of the de novo biosynthetic pathway for firefly luciferin remain unknown.
source: Of particular importance, the enzymes of the de novo biosynthetic pathway for firefly luciferin remain unknown (Oba et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oba et al., 2013b.

claim: Both luciferase and luciferin sulfotransferase (LST) were recovered as candidate genes using HE, DE, enzyme, and direct orthology criteria.
source: Both luciferase and luciferin sulfotransferase (LST), a specialized enzyme recently implicated in luciferin storage in P. pyralis (Fallon et al., 2016), were recovered as candidate genes using four criteria (HE, DE, enzymes, direct orthology across species), confirming the validity of our approach.
evidence: This is based on expression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: A direct ortholog of LST is present in A. lateralis.
source: While a direct ortholog of LST is present in A. lateralis, it is absent from I. luminosus, suggesting that LST, and the presumed luciferin storage it mediates, is an exclusive ancestral firefly or cantharoid trait.
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis.

claim: LST is absent from I. luminosus.
source: While a direct ortholog of LST is present in A. lateralis, it is absent from I. luminosus, suggesting that LST, and the presumed luciferin storage it mediates, is an exclusive ancestral firefly or cantharoid trait.
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis.

claim: LST, and the presumed luciferin storage it mediates, is an exclusive ancestral firefly or cantharoid trait.
source: While a direct ortholog of LST is present in A. lateralis, it is absent from I. luminosus, suggesting that LST, and the presumed luciferin storage it mediates, is an exclusive ancestral firefly or cantharoid trait.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence/absence pattern of LST.

claim: Adenylate kinase likely plays a critical role in efficient recycling of AMP post-luminescence.
source: For instance, adenylate kinase likely plays a critical role in efficient recycling of AMP post-luminescence, and cystathionine gamma-lyase supports a key role of cysteine in luciferin biosynthesis (Oba et al., 2013b) and recycling (Okada et al., 1974).
evidence: This is an inference based on the enzyme's known function and its enrichment in the lantern.

claim: Cystathionine gamma-lyase supports a key role of cysteine in luciferin biosynthesis and recycling.
source: For instance, adenylate kinase likely plays a critical role in efficient recycling of AMP post-luminescence, and cystathionine gamma-lyase supports a key role of cysteine in luciferin biosynthesis (Oba et al., 2013b) and recycling (Okada et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oba et al., 2013b and Okada et al., 1974, and by the enzyme's enrichment in the lantern.

claim: A combined adenylyl-sulfate kinase and sulfate adenylyltransferase enzyme (ASKSA) was detected among the lantern-enriched gene list.
source: We also detected a combined adenylyl-sulfate kinase and sulfate adenylyltransferase enzyme (ASKSA) among the lantern-enriched gene list (Appendix 4—figure 8), implicating active biosynthesis of 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS), the cofactor of LST, in the lantern.
evidence: This is based on expression analysis.

claim: ASKSA implicates active biosynthesis of 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS), the cofactor of LST, in the lantern.
source: We also detected a combined adenylyl-sulfate kinase and sulfate adenylyltransferase enzyme (ASKSA) among the lantern-enriched gene list (Appendix 4—figure 8), implicating active biosynthesis of 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS), the cofactor of LST, in the lantern.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enzyme's known function and its enrichment in the lantern.

claim: The firefly orthologs of ASKSA are the only members amongst their paralogs to contain a PTS1.
source: These firefly orthologs of ASKSA are the only members amongst their paralogs to contain a PTS1 (Appendix 4—figure 8), suggesting specialized localization to the peroxisome, the location of the luminescence reaction.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The firefly ASKSA orthologs have specialized localization to the peroxisome, the location of the luminescence reaction.
source: These firefly orthologs of ASKSA are the only members amongst their paralogs to contain a PTS1 (Appendix 4—figure 8), suggesting specialized localization to the peroxisome, the location of the luminescence reaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of PTS1 signal.

claim: The levels of sulfoluciferin and luciferin may be actively regulated within the peroxisome of lantern cells in response to luminescence.
source: This suggests that the levels of sulfoluciferin and luciferin may be actively regulated within the peroxisome of lantern cells in response to luminescence.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of PAPS biosynthesis enzymes in the lantern.

claim: Several directly orthologous enzymes share expression patterns in the light organs of both P. pyralis and A. lateralis.
source: Overall, our findings of several directly orthologous enzymes that share expression patterns in the light organs of both P. pyralis and A. lateralis suggests that the enzymatic physiology and/or the gene expression patterns of the photocytes were already fixed in the Luciolinae-Lampyrinae ancestor.
evidence: This is based on expression analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The enzymatic physiology and/or the gene expression patterns of the photocytes were already fixed in the Luciolinae-Lampyrinae ancestor.
source: Overall, our findings of several directly orthologous enzymes that share expression patterns in the light organs of both P. pyralis and A. lateralis suggests that the enzymatic physiology and/or the gene expression patterns of the photocytes were already fixed in the Luciolinae-Lampyrinae ancestor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of expression patterns.

claim: The abundant but as yet unidentified 'differentiated zone granule' organelles of the firefly light organ could be lysosomes.
source: We also performed a similar expression analysis for genes not annotated as enzymes, yielding several genes with predicted lysosomal function (Appendix 4—table 6; Appendix 4.4). This suggests that the abundant but as yet unidentified 'differentiated zone granule' organelles of the firefly light organ (Ghiradella and Schmidt, 2004) could be lysosomes.
evidence: This is speculation based on expression of lysosomal genes in the lantern.

claim: A highly expressed and differentially expressed opsin, Rh7, was found in the light organ of A. lateralis, but not P. pyralis.
source: Interestingly, we found a HE (TPM value ~300) and DE opsin, Rh7, in the light organ of A. lateralis, but not P. pyralis (Appendix 4—figure 9; Appendix 4.5), suggesting a potential light perception role for Rh7 in the A. lateralis lantern, akin to the light perception role described for Drosophila Rh7 (Ni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on expression analysis.

claim: Rh7 may have a potential light perception role in the A. lateralis lantern.
source: Interestingly, we found a HE (TPM value ~300) and DE opsin, Rh7, in the light organ of A. lateralis, but not P. pyralis (Appendix 4—figure 9; Appendix 4.5), suggesting a potential light perception role for Rh7 in the A. lateralis lantern, akin to the light perception role described for Drosophila Rh7 (Ni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on expression data and analogy to Drosophila Rh7.

claim: Firefly bioluminescence is postulated to have first evolved as an aposematic warning of larval chemical defenses.
source: Firefly bioluminescence is postulated to have first evolved as an aposematic warning of larval chemical defenses (Branham and Wenzel, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Branham and Wenzel, 2003.

claim: Lucibufagins are abundant unpalatable defense steroids described from certain North American firefly species.
source: Lucibufagins are abundant unpalatable defense steroids described from certain North American firefly species, most notably in the genera Photinus (Meinwald et al., 1979), Lucidota (Gronquist et al., 2005), and Ellychnia (Smedley et al., 2017), and hence are candidates for ancestral firefly defense compounds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meinwald et al., 1979, Gronquist et al., 2005, and Smedley et al., 2017.

claim: Lucibufagins were found in high abundance in P. pyralis adult hemolymph.
source: While lucibufagins were found in high abundance in P. pyralis adult hemolymph, they were not observed in A. lateralis adult hemolymph, nor in I. luminosus metathorax extract (Figure 6B; Appendix 4.6).
evidence: This is based on LC-HRAM-MS data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Lucibufagins were not observed in A. lateralis adult hemolymph.
source: While lucibufagins were found in high abundance in P. pyralis adult hemolymph, they were not observed in A. lateralis adult hemolymph, nor in I. luminosus metathorax extract (Figure 6B; Appendix 4.6).
evidence: This is based on LC-HRAM-MS data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Lucibufagins were not observed in I. luminosus metathorax extract.
source: While lucibufagins were found in high abundance in P. pyralis adult hemolymph, they were not observed in A. lateralis adult hemolymph, nor in I. luminosus metathorax extract (Figure 6B; Appendix 4.6).
evidence: This is based on LC-HRAM-MS data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Lucibufagins were found in P. pyralis larval extracts.
source: We found lucibufagins in P. pyralis larval extracts; however, they were not observed in A. lateralis larval extracts (Figure 6B; Appendix 4.6).
evidence: This is based on LC-HRAM-MS data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Lucibufagins were not observed in A. lateralis larval extracts.
source: We found lucibufagins in P. pyralis larval extracts; however, they were not observed in A. lateralis larval extracts (Figure 6B; Appendix 4.6).
evidence: This is based on LC-HRAM-MS data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The lucibufagin biosynthetic pathway is either a derived trait only found in particular firefly taxa (e.g. subfamily: Lampyrinae), or lucibufagin biosynthesis was an ancestral trait that was lost in A. lateralis.
source: Together, these results suggest that the lucibufagin biosynthetic pathway is either a derived trait only found in particular firefly taxa (e.g. subfamily: Lampyrinae), or that lucibufagin biosynthesis was an ancestral trait that was lost in A. lateralis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence/absence pattern of lucibufagins.

claim: The presence of lucibufagins in non-North-American Lampyrinae has been previously reported.
source: Consistent with the former hypothesis, the presence of lucibufagins in non-North-American Lampyrinae has been previously reported (Tyler et al., 2008), but to date there are no reports of lucibufagins in the Luciolinae.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tyler et al., 2008.

claim: To date there are no reports of lucibufagins in the Luciolinae.
source: Consistent with the former hypothesis, the presence of lucibufagins in non-North-American Lampyrinae has been previously reported (Tyler et al., 2008), but to date there are no reports of lucibufagins in the Luciolinae.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the literature.

claim: The results reject lucibufagins as ancestral defense compounds of fireflies.
source: Our results reject lucibufagins as ancestral defense compounds of fireflies, but rather suggest them as a derived metabolic trait associated with Lampyrinae.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chemical analysis data.

claim: Lucibufagins are suggested as a derived metabolic trait associated with Lampyrinae.
source: Our results reject lucibufagins as ancestral defense compounds of fireflies, but rather suggest them as a derived metabolic trait associated with Lampyrinae.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chemical analysis data.

claim: P. pyralis shows a unique CYP303 family expansion.
source: Our analysis revealed a unique expansion of one P450 family, the CYP303 family, in P. pyralis.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 94/97 of currently sequenced winged-insect genomes on OrthoDB contain only a single CYP303 family gene.
source: While 94/97 of currently sequenced winged-insect genomes on OrthoDB (Zdobnov et al., 2017), as well as the A. lateralis and I. luminosus genomes, contain only a single CYP303 family gene, the P. pyralis genome contains 11 CYP303 genes and two pseudogenes (Figure 6C), which expanded via tandem duplication on the same linkage group (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis with OrthoDB data.

claim: The A. lateralis and I. luminosus genomes contain only a single CYP303 family gene.
source: While 94/97 of currently sequenced winged-insect genomes on OrthoDB (Zdobnov et al., 2017), as well as the A. lateralis and I. luminosus genomes, contain only a single CYP303 family gene, the P. pyralis genome contains 11 CYP303 genes and two pseudogenes (Figure 6C), which expanded via tandem duplication on the same linkage group (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The P. pyralis genome contains 11 CYP303 genes and two pseudogenes.
source: While 94/97 of currently sequenced winged-insect genomes on OrthoDB (Zdobnov et al., 2017), as well as the A. lateralis and I. luminosus genomes, contain only a single CYP303 family gene, the P. pyralis genome contains 11 CYP303 genes and two pseudogenes (Figure 6C), which expanded via tandem duplication on the same linkage group (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on gene annotation and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The P. pyralis CYP303 genes expanded via tandem duplication on the same linkage group.
source: While 94/97 of currently sequenced winged-insect genomes on OrthoDB (Zdobnov et al., 2017), as well as the A. lateralis and I. luminosus genomes, contain only a single CYP303 family gene, the P. pyralis genome contains 11 CYP303 genes and two pseudogenes (Figure 6C), which expanded via tandem duplication on the same linkage group (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on genomic location analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The D. melanogaster CYP303 ortholog, CYP303A1, has been shown to play a role in mechanosensory bristle development.
source: The CYP303 ortholog of D. melanogaster, CYP303A1, has been shown to play a role in mechanosensory bristle development (Willingham and Keil, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Willingham and Keil, 2004.

claim: The exact biochemical function and substrate of D. melanogaster CYP303A1 is unknown.
source: Although the exact biochemical function and substrate of D. melanogaster CYP303A1 is unknown, its closely related P450 families operate on an insect steroid hormone ecdysone (Willingham and Keil, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Closely related P450 families to CYP303A1 operate on an insect steroid hormone ecdysone.
source: Although the exact biochemical function and substrate of D. melanogaster CYP303A1 is unknown, its closely related P450 families operate on an insect steroid hormone ecdysone (Willingham and Keil, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Willingham and Keil, 2004.

claim: The lineage-specific expansion of the CYP303 family in P. pyralis is a compelling candidate in the metabolic evolution of lucibufagins.
source: Therefore, the lineage-specific expansion of the CYP303 family in P. pyralis is a compelling candidate in the metabolic evolution of lucibufagins as chemical defenses associated with the aposematic role of bioluminescence.
evidence: This is speculation based on the correlation between CYP303 expansion and lucibufagin presence.

claim: The CYP303 expansion in P. pyralis may be associated with other lineage-specific chemical traits, such as pheromone production.
source: Alternatively, this CYP303 expansion in P. pyralis may be associated with other lineage-specific chemical traits, such as pheromone production.
evidence: This is an alternative speculation.

claim: Whole genome sequencing of wild-caught and laboratory reared fireflies revealed a rich microbiome.
source: Whole genome sequencing of our wild-caught and laboratory reared fireflies revealed a rich microbiome.
evidence: This is based on metagenomic analysis of sequencing data.

claim: Various bacterial genomes, viral genomes, and the complete mtDNA for a phorid parasitoid fly, Apocephalus antennatus, were found amongst the firefly genomes.
source: Amongst our firefly genomes, we found various bacterial genomes, viral genomes, and the complete mtDNA for a phorid parasitoid fly, Apocephalus antennatus, the first mtDNA reported for genus Apocephalus.
evidence: This is based on metagenomic analysis of sequencing data.

claim: This is the first mtDNA reported for genus Apocephalus.
source: Amongst our firefly genomes, we found various bacterial genomes, viral genomes, and the complete mtDNA for a phorid parasitoid fly, Apocephalus antennatus, the first mtDNA reported for genus Apocephalus.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding.

claim: The A. antennatus mtDNA was inadvertently included in the P. pyralis PacBio library via undetected parasitization of the initial specimens.
source: This mtDNA was inadvertently included in the P. pyralis PacBio library via undetected parasitization of the initial specimens, and was assembled via a metagenomic approach (Appendix 5.2).
evidence: This explains the source of the parasitoid mtDNA.

claim: This assembly provides the first complete genomic assembly of any Entomoplasma species.
source: Entomoplasma spp. were first isolated from the guts of North American fireflies (Hackett et al., 1992) and our assembly provides the first complete genomic assembly of any Entomoplasma species.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding.

claim: Broad read coverage for the E. luminosus subsp. pyralis genome was detected in 5/6 of the P. pyralis DNA libraries.
source: Broad read coverage for the E. luminosus subsp. pyralis genome was detected in 5/6 of our P. pyralis DNA libraries, suggesting that Entomplasma is a highly prevalent, possibly vertically inherited, P. pyralis symbiont.
evidence: This is based on read mapping analysis.

claim: Entomoplasma is a highly prevalent, possibly vertically inherited, P. pyralis symbiont.
source: Broad read coverage for the E. luminosus subsp. pyralis genome was detected in 5/6 of our P. pyralis DNA libraries, suggesting that Entomplasma is a highly prevalent, possibly vertically inherited, P. pyralis symbiont.
evidence: This is an inference based on the prevalence of the symbiont across libraries.

claim: It has been hypothesized that Entomoplasma mollicutes could play a role in firefly metabolism, specifically via contributing to cholesterol metabolism and lucibufagin biosynthesis.
source: It has been hypothesized that these Entomoplasma mollicutes could play a role in firefly metabolism, specifically via contributing to cholesterol metabolism and lucibufagin biosynthesis (Smedley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smedley et al., 2017.

claim: 43 scaffolds (2.3 Mbp; GC:29.8%, ~64x coverage) in the unfiltered A. lateralis genomic assembly were annotated as Tenericutes.
source: Within our unfiltered A. lateralis genomic assembly (Alat1.2), we also found 43 scaffolds (2.3 Mbp; GC:29.8%, ~64x coverage), whose taxonomic annotation corresponded to the Tenericutes (Appendix 2.5.2), suggesting that A. lateralis may also harbor a mollicute symbiont.
evidence: This is based on taxonomic annotation of assembly scaffolds.

claim: A. lateralis may also harbor a mollicute symbiont.
source: Within our unfiltered A. lateralis genomic assembly (Alat1.2), we also found 43 scaffolds (2.3 Mbp; GC:29.8%, ~64x coverage), whose taxonomic annotation corresponded to the Tenericutes (Appendix 2.5.2), suggesting that A. lateralis may also harbor a mollicute symbiont.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of Tenericutes sequences.

claim: Alat1.2 contains 2119 scaffolds (13.0 Mbp, GC:63.7%, ~25x coverage) annotated as of Proteobacterial origin.
source: Alat1.2 also contains 2119 scaffolds (13.0 Mbp, GC:63.7%, ~25x coverage) annotated as of Proteobacterial origin.
evidence: This is based on taxonomic annotation of assembly scaffolds.

claim: Limited Proteobacterial symbionts were detected in the I. luminosus assembly (0.4 Mbp; GC:30–65% ~10x coverage).
source: Limited Proteobacterial symbionts were detected in the I. luminosus assembly (0.4 Mbp; GC:30–65% ~10x coverage) (Appendix 3.5.2), suggesting no stable symbiont is present in adult I. luminosus.
evidence: This is based on taxonomic annotation of assembly scaffolds.

claim: No stable symbiont is present in adult I. luminosus.
source: Limited Proteobacterial symbionts were detected in the I. luminosus assembly (0.4 Mbp; GC:30–65% ~10x coverage) (Appendix 3.5.2), suggesting no stable symbiont is present in adult I. luminosus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited symbiont sequences detected.

claim: Two species of novel orthomyxoviridae-like ssRNA viruses, Photinus pyralis orthomyxo-like virus 1 and 2 (PpyrOMLV1/2), were detected.
source: Lastly, we detected two species of novel orthomyxoviridae-like ssRNA viruses, which we dub Photinus pyralis orthomyxo-like virus 1 and 2 (PpyrOMLV1/2), that were highly prevalent across our P. pyralis RNA-Seq datasets, and showed multi-generational transovarial transmission in the laboratory (Appendix 5.4).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: PpyrOMLV1/2 were highly prevalent across P. pyralis RNA-Seq datasets.
source: Lastly, we detected two species of novel orthomyxoviridae-like ssRNA viruses, which we dub Photinus pyralis orthomyxo-like virus 1 and 2 (PpyrOMLV1/2), that were highly prevalent across our P. pyralis RNA-Seq datasets, and showed multi-generational transovarial transmission in the laboratory (Appendix 5.4).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: PpyrOMLV1/2 showed multi-generational transovarial transmission in the laboratory.
source: Lastly, we detected two species of novel orthomyxoviridae-like ssRNA viruses, which we dub Photinus pyralis orthomyxo-like virus 1 and 2 (PpyrOMLV1/2), that were highly prevalent across our P. pyralis RNA-Seq datasets, and showed multi-generational transovarial transmission in the laboratory (Appendix 5.4).
evidence: This is based on laboratory observations.

claim: Several endogenous viral elements (EVEs) for PpyrOMLV1/2 were found in P. pyralis.
source: We also found several endogenous viral elements (EVEs) for PpyrOMLV1/2 in P. pyralis (Appendix 5.5).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: These viruses are the first reported in any firefly species.
source: These viruses are the first reported in any firefly species, and represent only the second report of transgenerational transfer of any Orthomyxoviridae virus (Marshall et al., 2014), and the second report of Orthomyxoviridae derived EVEs (Katzourakis and Gifford, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding.

claim: This represents only the second report of transgenerational transfer of any Orthomyxoviridae virus.
source: These viruses are the first reported in any firefly species, and represent only the second report of transgenerational transfer of any Orthomyxoviridae virus (Marshall et al., 2014), and the second report of Orthomyxoviridae derived EVEs (Katzourakis and Gifford, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marshall et al., 2014.

claim: This represents the second report of Orthomyxoviridae derived EVEs.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Katzourakis and Gifford, 2010.

claim: The genomic resources shared will facilitate the development of effective population genomic tools to monitor and protect wild bioluminescent beetle populations.
source: Finally, we hope that the genomic resources shared here will facilitate the development of effective population genomic tools to monitor and protect wild bioluminescent beetle populations in the face of changing climate and habitats.
evidence: This is a statement of anticipated future utility.

claim: The independent origins of the firefly and click beetle luciferases provide an exemplary natural model system to understand enzyme evolution through parallel mutational trajectories.
source: The independent origins of the firefly and click beetle luciferases provide an exemplary natural model system to understand enzyme evolution through parallel mutational trajectories and the evolution of complex metabolic traits generally.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: The abundance of gene duplication events of PACSs and ACSs at the ancestral luciferase locus suggests that ancestral promiscuous enzymatic activities served as raw materials for the selection of new adaptive catalytic functions.
source: The abundance of gene duplication events of PACSs and ACSs at the ancestral luciferase locus in both fireflies and I. luminosus suggests that ancestral promiscuous enzymatic activities served as raw materials for the selection of new adaptive catalytic functions (Weng, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed gene duplication patterns, supported by citation to Weng, 2014.

claim: Subtraits presumably dependent on an efficient luciferase, such as specialized tissues and neural control, almost certainly arose well after luciferase specialization.
source: While subtraits presumably dependent on an efficient luciferase, such as specialized tissues and neural control, almost certainly arose well after luciferase specialization, and thus can be inferred to also have independent origins between fireflies and click beetles, luciferin, which was presumably a prerequisite to luciferase neofunctionalization, may have been present in their common ancestor.
evidence: This is an inference about the evolutionary sequence of trait acquisition.

claim: Luciferin, which was presumably a prerequisite to luciferase neofunctionalization, may have been present in the common ancestor of fireflies and click beetles.
source: While subtraits presumably dependent on an efficient luciferase, such as specialized tissues and neural control, almost certainly arose well after luciferase specialization, and thus can be inferred to also have independent origins between fireflies and click beetles, luciferin, which was presumably a prerequisite to luciferase neofunctionalization, may have been present in their common ancestor.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary history of luciferin.

claim: Microbial endosymbionts, such as the tenericutes detected in P. pyralis and A. lateralis datasets, are intriguing candidate contributors to luciferin metabolism and biosynthesis.
source: Microbial endosymbionts, such as the tenericutes detected in our P. pyralis and A. lateralis datasets, are intriguing candidate contributors to luciferin metabolism and biosynthesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of symbionts.

claim: Firefly luciferin is readily produced non-enzymatically by mixing benzoquinone and cysteine.
source: Alternatively, recent reports have shown that firefly luciferin is readily produced non-enzymatically by mixing benzoquinone and cysteine (Kanie et al., 2016), and that a compound resulting from the spontaneous coupling of benzoquinone and cysteine acts as a luciferin biosynthetic intermediate in A. lateralis (Kanie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanie et al., 2016 and Kanie et al., 2018.

claim: A compound resulting from the spontaneous coupling of benzoquinone and cysteine acts as a luciferin biosynthetic intermediate in A. lateralis.
source: Alternatively, recent reports have shown that firefly luciferin is readily produced non-enzymatically by mixing benzoquinone and cysteine (Kanie et al., 2016), and that a compound resulting from the spontaneous coupling of benzoquinone and cysteine acts as a luciferin biosynthetic intermediate in A. lateralis (Kanie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kanie et al., 2018.

claim: Benzoquinone is known to be a defense compound of distantly related beetles and other arthropods.
source: Benzoquinone is known to be a defense compound of distantly related beetles (Dettner, 1987) and other arthropods (e.g. millipedes) (Shear, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dettner, 1987 and Shear, 2015.

claim: The adaptive light production of the primordial firefly that enabled the selection and neofunctionalization of luciferase was perhaps linked to a response to predators by a primitive whole-body oxygen-gated luminescence.
source: The adaptive light production of the primordial firefly (or alternatively, a primordial bioluminescent cantharoid beetle) that enabled the selection and neofunctionalization of luciferase was perhaps linked to a response to predators by a primitive whole-body oxygen-gated luminescence, where a startle-response mediated increase in hemolymph oxygenation through spiracle opening and escape locomotion caused a concomitant increase in luminescence (Buck and Case, 2002; Case, 2004).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Buck and Case, 2002 and Case, 2004.

claim: An early role for firefly luminescence in mate attraction has not been ruled out.
source: Alternatively, an early role for firefly luminescence in mate attraction has not been ruled out (Buck and Case, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buck and Case, 2002.

claim: The recently published Pyrocoelia pectoralis Lampyrinae firefly genome is an important advance which will contribute to future phylogenetic and evolutionary studies.
source: Toward this goal, the recently published Pyrocoelia pectoralis Lampyrinae firefly genome is an important advance which will contribute to future phylogenetic and evolutionary studies (Fu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 2017.
